items.title: Allen Toussaint Interview, 1979-03-13
items.q: And I do say New Orleans because we've been through Roy Browns, Bad Dominoes, etc. Lure Armstrongs, Al Hurts. So we've had giants in the world.

ctx.x: We're discussing the reasons for, and I've just learned that they're really too diverse to lump them all together. Bonnie Raitt, the Mighty Diamonds, and Robert Palmer. Trying to find out what attracts them to the studio and what's made the studio really a musical center in the recording industry of the world.

Well, New Orleans, for one. And probably first. New Orleans. New Orleans. New Orleans 19, so and so. Just whoever's in existence at that time. And I do say New Orleans because we've been through Roy Browns, Bad Dominoes, etc. Lure Armstrongs, Al Hurts. So we've had giants in the world. And there's, it is a birthplace for a lot of things. So New Orleans is already attractive, the sound of it, the music. Bonnie Raitt is well-versed, I guess, if you know Bonnie Raitt at all. Yes, love her music. In all mundane and…
Did you write Good Enough for Bonnie Raitt specifically? On her home plate album, the song Good Enough? Yeah. So you'd written that before she picked it up?

items.title: Allen Toussaint Interview, 1978-04-20
items.q: Melvin Lasky's father was from the same way song as Louis Armstrong.

ctx.x: Test one, two, test one, two.

Excuse me. And they began playing very, very experimental music. This was around 1949, maybe 1950. I'm not always so sure on these dates and things, but it's said to be 1949 in the book. They also misspelled the Melvin Lasky's name in the book and called him a clarinetist instead of a cornetist. So I have my doubts about what I read in some books. Anyhow, it was a... They were playing very free avant-garde music. It was also firmly based in the New Orleans tradition. Ed Blackwell, the first drummer in the quartet…
